questions.prompt: What is the primary detection signature of a domain generation algorithm?
options: A high NXDOMAIN rate from a single host, since most generated domains were never registered
questions.explanation: DGA detection keys on failure rather than success -- the malware tries many generated names, nearly all of which do not exist, before finding the one the operator registered.

questions.prompt: Why does Sysmon Event ID 22 change what you can conclude from DNS data?
options: It captures the full DNS response payload
It attributes the query to a specific process, turning 'this host resolved a suspicious domain' into 'this process did'
It works without any DNS server present
questions.explanation: Server-side DNS logs identify a client host. Process attribution is what elevates a lead into a finding, since rundll32.exe resolving a domain means something a host-level record cannot express.

questions.prompt: Why does DNS over HTTPS defeat the analysis in this lesson?
options: It encrypts the query name with a key only the attacker holds
The query travels as HTTPS to a public resolver, so the internal DNS server never sees it and query logs never record it
It changes the DNS protocol version
It only works for malicious domains
questions.explanation: Because DoH bypasses internal resolvers entirely, detection shifts to the connection layer -- HTTPS to known DoH endpoints, particularly from non-browser processes.

questions.prompt: Why does jitter fail to fully conceal beaconing?
options: Jitter is rarely implemented in real malware
Jitter widens the distribution of inter-arrival times rather than removing the pattern, so low-variance analysis still surfaces it
Jitter only affects the first callback
questions.explanation: Randomized delay of 20-30% remains statistically visible when inter-arrival times are computed across many queries to the same domain.
